problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as forecasting and decision-making in financial markets, specifically comparing quantum and classical machine learning on directional return prediction, live-trading simulation, and realized volatility forecasting. It asks whether, given identical inputs, quantum ML models can deliver more accurate forecasts or better trading outcomes than classical counterparts.
problem_statement_quotes:
Comprehensive QML vs Classical ML Benchmarking: Given identical inputs, do 
quantum ML models deliver more accurate forecasts than classical ones?

we present a reproducible
benchmarking framework that systematically compares
QML models with architecture-matched classical counter-
parts across three financial tasks: (i) directional return
prediction on U.S. and Turkish equities, (ii) live-trading
simulation with Quantum LSTMs versus classical LSTMs
on the S&P 500, and (iii) realized volatility forecasting using
Quantum Support Vector Regression.

Our methodology involves constructing three studies
that compare QML models with traditional ML models;
(i) Directional Classification which predicts whether a
stock’s price will rise or fall the next day (ii) Live trading
which tests how well a model decides when to buy or
sell the share of stocks to maximize cumulative profit
and (iii) Volatility forecasting which estimates the size
of price swings over a chosen horizon.
classical_baseline: The classical baselines are architecture-matched machine learning and econometric methods: ANNs for directional classification, LSTMs for live trading, SVR for volatility forecasting, and GARCH as an additional standard baseline for volatility. The paper treats these as the established methods to compare against the quantum models.
classical_baseline_quotes:
QNNs are evaluated against ANNs for Directional
Classification, QLSTMs against LSTMs for live trading,
and QSVRs against kernel SVRs for volatility
forecasting.

We benchmark QSVR against classical SVR and a standard
econometric baseline, GARCH(1,1).

As a point of comparison, we include the
GARCH(1,1) model, which is a standard economet-
ric approach for volatility forecasting.
classical_difficulty: The paper says classical methods can be limited by linearity, nonlinear market structure, overfitting in low-data regimes, poor generalization under market shifts, and feature-engineering demands. For volatility, it says standard linear time-series models fail to capture changing variance over time, and that kernel methods are used because linear SVR is limited in capturing nonlinear dependencies.
classical_difficulty_quotes:
However, they typically
rely on linear relationships and may struggle to capture
nonlinear interactions observed in real-world markets.

ML models are not without their tradeoffs: they can
suffer from overfitting in low-data regimes, struggle to
generalize under drastic market shifts, and often require
extensive feature engineering.

In financial markets, Mandelbrot (1963) [42] was the
first to observe that large changes tend to be followed
by large changes and small changes by small changes
regardless of the direction. This phenomenon, known
as volatility clustering [43], means that standard lin-
ear time-series models like Autoregressive Integrated
Moving Average (ARIMA) [44] fail to capture the
changing variance over time since they typically assume
homoscedastic errors.

While linear SVR is effective when the relationship between input
features and the target is approximately linear, it is
limited in its ability to capture nonlinear dependencies [68].
business_stakes: The paper explicitly ties the tasks to trading signals, portfolio exposure, transaction costs, and risk-adjusted profitability. It says directional models are used for basic trading and risk signals, volatility forecasting informs position sizing and risk management, and live trading is evaluated net of trading costs and against buy-and-hold.

ing forecasts into trading decisions.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; paper is a benchmark study with clear classical baselines and trading/risk framing.
